..
Issued at 252 AM EDT Fri Oct 16 2026

Midnight KMQT radar shows widespread rainfall but with more 
striation patterns occurring with time to indicated mesoscale bands 
forming. These bands will lead to some spatial variation in the 
rainfall totals by the time synoptic rainfall ends this morning and 
we transition to a lake effect rainfall pattern. At the surface, a 
1005mb low is traversing the Lower Peninsula with a strengthening 
pressure gradient over the Dakotas as 1040mb high pressure moves 
over the MT/WY/SD tripoint. Aloft, the low is supported by a 
positively tilted 500mb trough centered over Minnesota and the high 
is supported by a ridge axis most prominent over the Canadian and 
northern US Rockies (which sits atop a monsoon trough over San 
Diego). With the positive tilt of the trough and the trough itself 
being tilted with respect to height above the surface low, the low 
will deepen as it moves east into this weekend, and despite the high 
weakening slightly with time, the strengthening low will keep the 
post-low pressure gradient strong. This will drive gusty winds, in 
conjunction with isallobaric winds (GFS shows up to 10mb/6hr rises 
today) and cold advection aloft will help mix down stronger winds 
aloft as well. Mean peak surface wind gusts in the HREF by noon 
today are 35-40 mph over land and 40-45 mph at and around Lake 
Superior as a result. On the precipitation side of things, the 
aforementioned cold advection will bring 850mb temperatures down to 
around -4 to -8 C over a Lake Superior that is around 10-12 C, 
inducing up to 200 J/kg of instability over eastern Lake Superior 
per the NAM. As ridging aloft spills into the Plains and high 
pressure advances towards the region, lake effect rain (and even a 
10-20% chance of the first few snowflakes of the season, no 
accumulation forecast) will gradually decrease in coverage and 
intensity, ending altogether Saturday. By 06Z Saturday, mean HREF 
QPF is highest (0.75"+) along an arc from the US41/US141 split, up 
to the Mount Arvon/Eagle Mine vicinity, and down to Palmer, with the 
areas surrounding this arc seeing around a half inch on average and 
the rest of the UP still seeing a wetting rain (about 0.1"-0.33"), 
though perhaps not enough to bust the drought. Still, 2 of the 3 
largest ongoing wildfires are within this arc, which the rain will 
help keep the fire behavior down, though it will also complicate 
access to the fire further (muddy roads, slick exposed rock, low 
ceilings for aviation support, etc). 

Despite rainfall ending Saturday, this weekend will still carry some 
weather impacts. Atop the advancing ridge will be a rapidly moving 
and compact trough passing through the northern portions of the
Canadian Prairie provinces into Hudson Bay. While the trough 
and resulting surface low will be too far away to deliver 
further precipitation to the UP for the back end of this 
weekend, the low (around 986 mb over western Hudson Bay Sunday 
afternoon per the GFS) will squeeze the pressure gradient 
tighter against the high pressure, which the GFS resolves at 
1035 mb over Pennsylvania Sunday afternoon. This results in Euro
ensemble mean gusts over the UP of 25-35 mph out of the 
southwest both afternoons of Saturday and Sunday, paired with 
LREF chances of sub-30% RHs at up to 25%. This combination of 
dry and windy weather could once again result in worsening 
wildfire weather conditions, though confidence on the RH 
forecast is low as well as low confidence in fuel moistures (the
main question being "was wet weather this week enough to 
moisten the fuels in a meaningful way?"), so the forecast 
continues to bear monitoring through the weekend.

More consistent ridging over central North America will bring 
quieter weather (continued lack of rainfall but this time with 
lighter winds) for the beginning of next week. Expect highs around 
the 60s (perhaps lower for the Keweenaw and Lake Superior shores) 
and lows around the freezing mark in the interior and 40s closer to 
the shores. The next batch of widespread rainfall appears to be with 
a trough that passes through the Canadian Prairie in the back half 
of the week, but differences in ensemble timing and intensity of the 
parent trough results in the peak in PoPs in the NBM being around 
35% Wednesday night into Thursday.
